title: FDE Client Simulation
description: 45-min role-play round. Interviewer plays a stressed customer. Practice: ownership language, diagnostic Qs BEFORE solutions, acknowledge valid points, explicit trade-off options, never over-promise.

questions.prompt: Deployment has slipped 3 weeks. The client's CTO is on the call, visibly frustrated. First 5 minutes.

rubric.criterion: Own it upfront: 'I take responsibility'; no shifting to third parties
State the fact concisely — what slipped, why, what's confirmed vs still uncertain
Ask 1-2 diagnostic questions about their operational pressure (customer commitments, revenue impact)
Present a REVISED plan with dates, not vague promises
Offer explicit trade-off options (ship narrower on original date vs. current scope on new date)
Sets a next check-in and a written summary in follow-up

questions.modelAnswer: I want to own this. We're three weeks behind on X because of [concrete cause]. Y is confirmed complete; Z is still at risk. Before I lay out the recovery plan, can you tell me what's most exposed on your side — any customer or board commitments tied to the original date? Two options: (a) we cut scope to just the top three flows and ship in one week, (b) we hold scope and land two-and-a-half weeks late with everything verified. I'll send a written summary of whichever you pick within the hour, and I'll be on this call every Friday at 3 until we ship.

questions.prompt: Client insists on a feature that would bypass their own governance policy. Push back without breaking the relationship.

rubric.criterion: Acknowledges the underlying need before objecting
Names the specific policy in plain terms
Explains the concrete risk (audit fail, breach, reputational)
Offers 1-2 alternative paths that meet the same need within policy
Doesn't moralize; escalates to their compliance team if needed

questions.modelAnswer: I hear you — you need X so your team can move faster on Y. Building it the way you described bypasses your data-classification policy Z. If we ship it and your auditor finds it, it's a bigger cleanup than the time we're saving. Two alternatives that get you to the same speed: [option A within policy], or [option B that requires your compliance team to sign off on a scoped exception]. I'll set up a 20-minute call with your compliance lead this week to walk through B — that's typically the fastest legit path.

questions.prompt: Non-technical VP wants a written guarantee of 100% accuracy from the LLM. How do you respond?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't sign the guarantee — under any framing
Explains why 100% is not achievable, in plain language
Reframes the ask: what business outcome are they protecting?
Proposes measurable SLOs + audit + human-in-the-loop for critical paths
Offers reversibility: rollback + kill switch as risk mitigators

questions.modelAnswer: I understand this needs to be safe enough to defend to your board. I can't sign 100% because no LLM system on the planet is 100% — anyone who signs that is either lying or hasn't shipped. What I CAN commit to is: an audit trail of every response, a 99.X% task-success SLO measured weekly, human review on any high-impact action, and a one-click rollback. If we agree the review is what makes it safe, we can add another line of defense with a policy-check gate. Can we walk through your two or three riskiest scenarios and design the guardrails around those?

questions.prompt: Client IT will not grant production credentials required for your integration. Unblock without circumventing security.

rubric.criterion: Asks WHY, not just what they need — surfaces the underlying concern
Proposes least-privilege credential scope; time-bound; rotated
Offers to work through their SSO / vault (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, CyberArk)
Suggests a phased approach: read-only first, write later after review
Willing to defer the production step if it means keeping the relationship + policy intact

questions.modelAnswer: Fair — production creds are exactly what should be hard to get. What's the specific policy or risk they're worried about? If it's blast-radius, we can start with read-only creds scoped to two tables, rotated weekly, checked out via your Vault. I don't need to hold them — the runtime pulls them at request time. If that's still too much, we can shadow in a lower-tier environment for two weeks and only ask for prod once we've shown zero drift. Who from their security team should I loop in?

questions.prompt: A client calls during a live demo — errors are appearing in front of their executive team. Handle it.

rubric.criterion: Composure — no panicking, no blame
Own it in the moment; the exec team hears an operator, not a victim
Buys time: switch to a known-good scenario or a pre-recorded fallback
Commits to a written follow-up with cause + fix within a stated window
Does NOT ship a hotfix live in front of the exec team

questions.modelAnswer: Live: 'That's a real error — I own it. Let's continue with [known-good scenario] so you can see what the end-to-end feel is, and I'll be back to you by end of day with the fix and what caused it.' Off-call: root-cause fast, write a short summary email to the exec + your champion by close of business. Don't hotfix in the demo. Follow up in the next scheduled sync with the fix deployed + why.

questions.prompt: Client demands a six-week feature in three days.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't say yes to keep the peace
Asks what problem the deadline solves — often the real ask is smaller
Offers a smaller-in-3-days + full-in-6-weeks split
Names what breaks if we try to compress: quality, tests, other commitments

questions.modelAnswer: Help me understand what's driving the three days — is it a specific meeting, an external commitment, or an internal deadline? If we compress, I can ship [thinnest slice that solves that specific thing] in three days, but the full feature stays six weeks — squeezing it further either misses the deadline anyway or ships something we'll have to rebuild. Which sounds better to you?

questions.prompt: You deployed a fix two hours ago. Client reports the same problem is back. They're losing confidence.

rubric.criterion: Owns the confidence problem, not just the bug
Doesn't debate whether it's 'the same' — treats their perception as data
Rolls back if uncertain rather than shipping fix #2
Names the process gap that let the first fix ship without full verification
Written post-mortem within 24 hours with what changes so it doesn't happen a third time

questions.modelAnswer: You're right — two fixes in two hours would erode my trust too. I'm rolling back the change now while I confirm root cause; better to be stable than fast. My process gap: I shipped based on a repro on my side without verifying the customer environment path. I'll have a written post-mortem to you by end of tomorrow with (1) what the actual cause was, (2) what verification would have caught it, (3) how our process changes so it doesn't happen a third time. I'll also propose a monitoring signal we should have had.

questions.prompt: Two teams inside the client (Data and IT) are blocking each other; your project is stalled between them.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't pick a side
Names the standoff to your exec sponsor before it becomes a delivery issue
Proposes a joint 30-min meeting with a specific decision on the agenda
Offers a technical middle path they can both accept (compromise architecture)
Documents the decision so it doesn't reopen

questions.modelAnswer: Sponsor: 'We're blocked between Data and IT on X — neither has veto, but neither will move without the other. I'll set up a 30-min meeting on Thursday with one decision on the agenda: [specific choice]. I'll bring a proposal that gives both sides most of what they want. Can you attend and back the decision that comes out?' Then run the meeting to a written decision; distribute same day.
